back: Analyzing the needs and characteristics of stakeholders to understand how best to identify, involve, communicate with and work with them.

Identify stakeholders; conduct stakeholder analysis; determine engagement and communication approach; conduct business analysis planning; prepare for transition to future state; manage engagement and communication; assess business analysis performance.
Identifying the individuals, groups or organizations that may impact, are impacted, or are perceived to be impacted by the area under assessment.
The list of stakeholders with their identification, assessment and classification. Kept up to date throughout.
Brainstorming, interviews, organizational charts, process flows, questionnaires and surveys.
Researching and analyzing quantitative and qualitative information about stakeholders, to choose techniques, timing and communication methods.

front: Characteristics recorded in a stakeholder register
back: Role, attitude, interests, level of impact, level of influence, communication preferences, success criteria, work hours and location.
Unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading.
A fictional character created to represent an individual or a class of users, with detail on how they work.
A persona is fictional and detailed about behavior. A stakeholder is a real person.
A group of stakeholders with similar characteristics, represented by a persona.
Identifying the requirements and competencies needed to perform a job or role. Useful when a solution changes or creates roles.
Responsible (does the task), Accountable (final approver), Consult (gives information), Inform (kept up to date).
Responsible performs the task. Accountable answers for its completion and quality and gives final approval.
A two-by-two grid for analyzing stakeholders on two chosen variables, for example influence and impact.
The critical group and a key source of requirements. Most effort, frequent communication, strong partnership.
Possible champions and advocates. Keep communication open and use their support.
Still a critical source of requirements: often those who must adapt to the solution. Make sure their concerns are heard.
Do not ignore. Monitor in case their relationship to the solution changes.
Rings around the solution showing how close each stakeholder is to it. Nearer the center means a stronger relationship.
Agreements on each stakeholder's involvement, how decisions and approvals are made, how information is stored, and how stakeholders are kept informed.

front: Conduct Business Analysis Planning: three things it does
back: Brings together the approaches from all knowledge areas; estimates the effort; assembles the business analysis plan.

front: Business analysis plan vs requirements management plan
back: The business analysis plan covers the whole approach and is broader. The requirements management plan covers only how requirements are handled.

front: Business analysis planning: predictive vs adaptive
back: Predictive: separate estimates per task, a plan approved before elicitation. Adaptive: effort not estimated separately, rarely a separate deliverable.
Near-term work is planned in detail; later work is planned at a higher level.

front: Prepare for Transition to Future State
back: Determining whether the organization is ready for a transition and how it will move from the current to the future state.
Determines the organization's ability and interest to move to the future state, and identifies gaps in readiness as risks.
Based on the readiness assessment and transition strategy. Covers communication, rollout, training, procedure updates and other transition requirements.
Massive one-time cutover; staged release; time-boxed coexistence; permanent coexistence.
Rolling out the future state one segment at a time: by region, customer type or user type.
Fostering appropriate involvement, keeping stakeholders informed, and sharing product information as it evolves.
Those who can remove roadblocks: the project manager, functional managers and the sponsor, who has the authority.
Considering how effective the business analysis practices are, so they can be adjusted.

front: When is business analysis performance assessed?
back: Predictive: at milestones or the end, as lessons learned. Adaptive: at least at the end of every iteration.

front: Stakeholder analysis: analyst vs project manager
back: The project manager looks at impact on the project; the analyst at impact on the solution. They should do it together.

front: Four layers of an onion diagram
back: 1: the team doing the work. 2: those directly impacted. 3: those who interact with layer 2. 4: external stakeholders.

front: C and D on the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix
back: C = current engagement, D = desired engagement. A gap between them needs action.
